source.title: Unified Defense for Large Language Models against Jailbreak and Fine-Tuning Attacks in Education
source.authors: Xin Yi; Yue Li; Dong-Sheng Shi; Lin-Lin Wang; Xiaoling Wang; Liang He

record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates harmful fine-tuning and jailbreak attacks and reports their effects on harmful-response rates, using an educational benchmark and attack settings rather than reproducing the original studies' full methods.
record.gate_note: The paper tests harmful fine-tuning at harmful-data ratios of 0%, 10% and 20% and evaluates multiple jailbreak strategies. It does not test benign fine-tuning against an un-fine-tuned reference, per-token KL, compliant-prefix prefill, or whether safety resides in a small set of weights. It also reports internal hidden-state patterns at instruction positions; these do not measure response-token KL or first-response-token concentration. Defense-method results are not extracted except for the Vanilla/SFT attack outcomes relevant to the claims.
record.test_reason: This is a defense paper, but it reports undefended (Vanilla/SFT) attack outcomes in a new educational setting (EduHarm). These include harmful-data SFT at p=0.1/0.2 versus clean SFT (V1) and adversarial-suffix attacks GCG/RandomSearch versus no attack (V4). That makes it a new-setting test (T3), not a same-question replication (T2).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude, from preliminary hidden-state analysis, that fine-tuning mainly weakens the refusal feature while the harmfulness feature at the instruction token stays intact. They use that feature as the detection signal for TSSF.
record.recipe_differences: The paper evaluates educational-domain attacks and a unified defense; harmful-data SFT uses a 1000-example mixture at p = 0, 0.1, and 0.2. It does not claim to replicate the original studies' recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack strategy and model change ASR substantially; harmful-data ratio changes fine-tuning ASR. The paper also reports that attention realignment hyperparameters affect ASR and benign compliance.

fits_no_version.finding: Hidden-state cluster tendency at the last instruction token versus the last template token differs by attack type and fine-tuning condition. Fine-tuning shifts the post-instruction (refusal) representation toward acceptance, while the instruction-token (harmfulness) representation stays in the refusal cluster.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful fine-tuning erodes the refusal signal at the post-instruction position while the harmfulness representation at the instruction token survives. This is a prompt-position finding, not response-position KL.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt-rewriting, role-play, encoding and obfuscation jailbreaks (PAIR, DeepInception, GPTfuzzer, Cipher, ArtPrompt, AutoDAN) raise ASR, to near 100% for some, across all three models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: General jailbreak susceptibility in educational-domain models; broader than V4's opening, suffix or decoding mechanism.

record.problems: The relevant ASR results report no uncertainty estimates. ASR is classified by GLM-4.5-Flash, rather than reported human judgments. The preliminary hidden-state analyses do not state the model identity in the supplied text, and their plotted values are not numerically given.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded defense-method ASR comparisons (Tables 1–4 and B.1–B.4) except the Vanilla/SFT results, because the defense methods are not the attacks or training effects named by the claim. Also excluded utility and latency metrics and TSSF hyperparameter ablations because they do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Only 100 and 200 harmful examples within 1000-example mixtures; no small-count sweep.
No clean-SFT vs un-fine-tuned comparison is presented as such. A cross-table comparison is possible but not confirmed to be on the same evaluation set.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No compliant-prefix prefill or decoding-change attacks. Suffix attacks were tested only on Qwen3-8B.
Not tested; TSSF is a detection/routing defense, not deepening.

missing.what: Qwen3-8B SFT ASR at p=0.2 by downstream task: AGNews 50.08, SST-2 48.28, GSM8K 88.51. This shows the harmful-fine-tuning effect depends on task.

No-attack ASR of the un-fine-tuned models (37.64/43.38/47.70) versus clean benign SFT ASR (33.05/33.91/37.07). Benign SFT appears not to raise, and may lower, ASR, but the two evaluations are not confirmed to use the same prompt set.
missing.locator: Table 1, B.1, B.2 vs Table 3, B.3, B.4

record.verdict_notes: The attack numbers are undefended baselines in a defense paper. ASR is judged by GLM-4.5-Flash with no uncertainty reported. The base models already reach 33–48% ASR on EduHarm without attack, so 'safety-trained' refusal is weak in this domain. V2 was not labelled because cross-table comparability is unverified. No result bears on V3, V5, V6 or V7.

versions.untested_parts: The harmful-data experiment uses 100 or 200 harmful examples among 1000 training examples; it does not test other harmful example counts or show refusal is removed for all models.
No comparison of benign fine-tuning with an otherwise matching un-fine-tuned model.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models, or measurement across response positions.
Tests jailbreak strategies, including GCG, but not compliant-opening prefills or decoding changes; it does not isolate the causal role of getting past initial response tokens.
No test that a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Does not test whether the data or training objective causes safety shallowness.
Does not train or evaluate a method intended to spread safety beyond initial response tokens.
